entries.narration: Before learning how Spark works, it is worth asking when you need it at all, because the honest answer is less often than people assume. The code on the left is plain pandas. It reads one day of a retailer's order events, keeps the completed orders, and sums the sales for each store. On a sample, this is exactly the right tool. It is short, it is easy to test, and nothing has to cross a network. Now apply the retailer's real numbers. About two hundred gigabytes of events arrive every day, and a year of history comes to roughly seventy terabytes. Do the arithmetic before deciding anything. At an assumed two gigabytes per second, one day scans in about a hundred seconds, so for the daily summary the real question is memory, not time. A full year takes around ten hours. Pandas holds its whole input in the memory of a single process, so the first limit is memory. The second is scan time, because one disk still has to read every byte. The third is the deadline, since the summary must be ready before the stores open. And the fourth is fragility: a crash near the end means starting again from the beginning. Distributed processing is justified when one of those limits is genuinely reached, and the work can be split into pieces that run independently. If a single machine meets the deadline, keep the single machine. Calling the data big is not a reason on its own; the deadline decides.

There are two ways to give a workload more capacity. Scaling up means a bigger machine: more cores, more memory, faster disks. Its great virtue is that nothing about the program changes. There is no network in the middle, and no partial failures to reason about. Its limit is a hard ceiling, the largest machine anyone will sell or rent you. Scaling out means adding machines instead, and that has no fixed ceiling. You can keep adding nodes as the data grows. Let's put numbers on it. Assume each machine can read about two gigabytes per second. Scanning the retailer's seventy terabytes of history then takes around thirty five thousand seconds, which is nearly ten hours, on one machine. Spread across fifty machines, the same scan is roughly twelve minutes. But notice the qualifier: before any overhead. Here is the common misconception. Scaling out is not automatically faster. The machines must agree on who reads what, results have to travel over the network, and somebody has to notice and recover when one node fails. For a small job, that coordination can cost more than the work itself. So the rule is simple. Scale up until a hard ceiling or the deadline forces you out, and scale out when the work is large enough to pay for the coordination it brings.

Once a workload is spread across machines, two ideas carry most of the weight. The first is the partition. The order events are still one logical dataset, but physically they are split into chunks, and each chunk can be processed without looking at any other. Here there are six partitions spread over three machines, so three pieces of work can run at the same moment. The second idea is locality. Distributed storage systems keep the blocks of a large file on many different machines, and the cheapest plan is to run the computation where the data already sits. Shipping a few kilobytes of program to a machine is fast. Shipping hundreds of gigabytes of events to the program is not. So in this picture, each machine sums the sales in the partitions it holds, and only those small partial totals cross the network to be combined. For store seven, machine A found twelve hundred in sales, machine B nine hundred and fifty, and machine C fourteen hundred and thirty, and adding the three gives the full total of three thousand five hundred and eighty. That is the shape to look for. Notice what it depends on, though. Summing is easy to split, because partial sums can simply be added together. Not every operation works that way. You cannot get a median by combining three partial medians, and you cannot add three distinct counts without double counting. When an operation has to bring all the records for one key together onto one machine, records must move between machines, and that movement is a cost the later chapters will learn to measure.

Spark did not arrive out of nowhere. Before it, the standard model for large batch processing was MapReduce. You split the input, a map function processes each piece, the framework shuffles the results so that everything with the same key lands together, and a reduce function combines them. That model made processing at this scale practical, and its ideas are still inside Spark. The trouble was what happened between jobs. Each MapReduce job wrote its output to replicated distributed storage, such as HDFS. So a task with several steps, like summing sales and then joining the result to store data, became a chain of separate jobs, and every link in the chain wrote its result out and read it straight back in. Iterative work, which revisits the same data many times, paid that cost on every pass. Spark grew out of research at UC Berkeley aimed at exactly this. One Spark program describes the whole sequence of steps, so the engine can plan them together, keep intermediate results inside the application, and cache data that is reused. Here is the misconception to avoid. Spark is not purely in memory. It still writes shuffle data to local disk, and it spills to disk when memory runs short. What it avoids is the round trip through replicated storage between every step.

To finish this chapter, let's be precise about what Spark is, and what it is not. Spark is a distributed compute engine. It takes a description of work, plans it, and runs it across many machines, over data that lives somewhere else. Within that role it covers a lot of ground: batch processing with DataFrames and SQL, incremental processing of arriving data with Structured Streaming, and reading and writing many data formats. Just as important is what it leaves to other systems. Spark does not store your data durably. Object stores, distributed file systems and databases do that. It runs on machines that a cluster manager provides. Transactional guarantees on tables come from table formats layered over storage. And deciding that a pipeline runs every night at two is the job of a scheduler. On the left is the pipeline this course returns to again and again. Order events arrive all day as JSON, alongside reference data for products and stores. The pipeline ingests the events with a declared schema, sets aside the malformed ones, enriches them with the reference data, and summarises daily sales per store, with a streaming view added later. Each stage maps onto a later chapter: ingestion and schemas in chapters three and four, cleaning in chapter four, enrichment joins in chapter four and their skew in chapter six, the summary's plans and shuffles in chapters five and six, and the live view in chapter seven. We can now justify distributing a workload like this one. Next, we trace what actually happens inside a small Spark application when it runs.

This chapter follows one small application from the first line to the last, so let's read it carefully before anything runs. It assumes Spark four point zero point one, which runs on Java seventeen or twenty one and Python three point nine or later. The master setting, local four, means everything runs on one machine with four worker threads, which is enough to show every idea in this chapter without a cluster. The application has four phases. First, get or create builds a Spark session, and with it the driver, the process that will plan and coordinate everything. Second, the application declares its work: read the day's order events with an explicit schema, keep the completed orders, and sum the sales per store. Third comes the write, and that is the line that actually does something. Fourth, stop releases the application's resources. Here is the assumption to drop straight away. It is natural to read this top to bottom and picture each line executing as it is reached. It doesn't. The read, the filter and the grouping only describe the computation. No order data is read until line seventeen, when the write asks for a result. The explicit schema matters too. Without it, Spark would have to scan the files just to discover their columns, and that scan would happen early. Over the next sections, we'll see who runs each part, and how one write becomes jobs, stages and tasks.

When the application starts, three roles appear. The driver is the process running your program. It holds the Spark session, the entry point you call, and behind it the Spark context, which connects to the cluster. The driver turns your code into a plan, breaks the plan into tasks, and schedules those tasks. The cluster manager is a separate service whose only job is allocating resources. In Spark four that is Spark's own standalone manager, YARN, or Kubernetes. Once resources are granted, Spark starts executors on the worker machines. Executors are processes that run tasks and can keep cached data in memory, and each application gets its own executors for its whole lifetime. They are not shared with other applications, which means two applications can only share data through external storage. In our local four setup, all of this collapses into a single JVM: the driver and one executor live together, and the four threads are the task slots. Now the misconception. Because your code runs in the driver, it is tempting to think the driver processes the data. It does not. The data stays on the executors, and the driver receives only what you ask for: a count, a small sample, or the confirmation that a write finished. That is why calling collect on a large result is dangerous. It pulls every row back into one process.

There are two ways for your code to reach a driver, and the difference matters for what you can call. In Classic Spark, which is what our local application uses, your Python process and the driver's JVM run side by side and talk through a bridge called Py4J. The Python objects are thin wrappers around objects living in the JVM. Spark Connect moves that boundary. The client becomes a thin library that never touches a JVM. When you build a DataFrame, it records an unresolved logical plan, encodes it with protocol buffers, and sends it to a Connect server over gRPC. The server, running inside a remote driver, analyses and executes the plan, and streams results back as Apache Arrow row batches. Look at what that costs the client. There is no RDD API, because the protocol describes logical plans, not low level execution. There is no Spark context, and no access to static configuration. In four point zero point one, asking a Connect session for its Spark context raises an error, and so does asking a DataFrame for its RDD. In return, operators gain isolation. A client that crashes or runs out of memory only hurts itself, and the server can be upgraded without rebuilding every application. Spark four also adds an API mode setting that runs a Classic application through a local Connect server. Because RDDs need Classic, this course's RDD examples assume it.

Every DataFrame operation falls into one of two kinds. A transformation, such as where, select, group by with an aggregation, or join, returns a new DataFrame and runs nothing at all. It just adds a step to the plan. An action, such as count, show, collect, or write, asks for an actual result, and only at that moment does Spark plan the work and run it. Why design it this way? Because by waiting, Spark sees the whole plan before choosing how to execute it. It can push a filter down toward the data source, and read only the columns the query needs, decisions it could not make one line at a time. Follow the code on the left. After the filter and the grouping, zero jobs have run. Then count is called, and a job reads the input. Then write is called, and here is the surprise for many people: the input is read again. Each action recomputes its plan from the source, unless you explicitly cache an intermediate result, which is a trade-off for a later chapter. One more contrast. It is tempting to say reading is always lazy, but that only holds when Spark already knows the schema. Read JSON without one, and Spark scans the input to infer the columns before you have called any action at all. With a day of order events, that is a full extra pass. This is why our application declares its schema.

In the first chapter, partitions were a storage idea. Here they become the unit of parallel work. Within a stage, Spark runs exactly one task per partition, and a task is what the driver sends to a free slot on an executor. By default, each executor core is one slot. Let's put the full retail workload through this. When Spark reads files, it packs at most one hundred and twenty eight megabytes into a partition. That is the default for spark dot sql dot files dot max partition bytes. So one day of order events, two hundred gigabytes, becomes roughly sixteen hundred input partitions, and therefore about sixteen hundred tasks in the first stage. Now give the job fifty executors with four cores each. That is two hundred slots, so the sixteen hundred tasks run in about eight waves of two hundred. Two rules fall out of this. At most one task runs per slot at a time, so slots cap the parallelism. And partitions cap it too. If there are fewer partitions than slots, the extra slots sit idle. The opposite extreme costs too: every task carries scheduling overhead, so thousands of tiny partitions spend their time being coordinated rather than computing. That leads to a common misconception: that adding executors always makes a job faster. Picture a stage with only four partitions. It runs four tasks, whether the cluster has four slots or four thousand. The number of partitions is a design decision, and later chapters show how to choose it from evidence.

There is one question that explains most of Spark's execution behaviour. For each step, does an output partition depend on one input partition, or on many? When it depends on one, the dependency is narrow. Filters, projections and new columns are all narrow. Each partition is transformed exactly where it already sits, and a chain of narrow steps can run back to back inside the same task, record by record, without writing anything in between. Spark calls that pipelining. When an output partition depends on many input partitions, the dependency is wide. Grouping with an aggregation, distinct, sorting, and most joins are wide, because rows that share a key may be scattered across every input partition and have to meet in one place. That redistribution is the shuffle. The output side of a DataFrame shuffle has two hundred partitions by default, set by spark dot sql dot shuffle dot partitions, and in Spark four adaptive query execution is on by default and can merge small ones at runtime. Some joins avoid the shuffle by broadcasting a small table, which a later chapter covers. Now the misconception. A group by does not have to send every order across the network. For a sum, each task first adds up its own rows per store, exactly like the partial totals in chapter one, and only those partial sums are shuffled. The shuffle still costs, but far less than moving raw events.

Now we can connect everything. When the write is called, the driver turns the plan into a graph of steps and submits a job. The job is divided into stages, and the dividing lines are the shuffles. Everything between two shuffles is narrow, so it can be pipelined, and each stage runs one task per partition, every task doing the same work on a different slice of the data. Apply that to the daily summary. Stage zero scans the order events, keeps the completed ones, and computes partial sums per store, all inside each task, so it runs about sixteen hundred tasks, one per input partition. Then comes the shuffle that the grouping requires. Stage one reads the shuffled partial sums, finishes the totals per store, and writes the Parquet files. It has at most two hundred tasks, the default shuffle partition count, and often fewer, because adaptive query execution can coalesce small partitions once it sees the real data sizes. A warning for when you open the Spark UI. With adaptive execution on, which is the default, a single action can appear as more than one job, and the number of tasks in a stage can differ from what you predicted on paper. So do not count stages by counting lines of code. Count the shuffles. Five lines of narrow transformations are still one stage. One group by is a new one.

Let's finish by tracing what happens when something goes wrong, because this is where the execution model pays off. Spark does not protect intermediate data by copying it to several machines. Instead, it relies on lineage. For every partition, it knows the chain of steps that produced it, so a lost partition can simply be computed again. Start with a single failed task, say a stage one task that hits a bad disk. The scheduler retries it, on a different executor if it can, and the job only fails if the same task fails four times in a row, the default for spark dot task dot max failures. One caveat: plain local mode gives each task a single attempt. You need a cluster, or the local four comma two form, to see retries. Now a bigger failure. Stage zero has finished, and its tasks have written shuffle files to their executors' local disks. Then executor two disappears, and its shuffle files go with it, unless an external shuffle service was keeping them. Stage one tries to fetch that data and fails. Spark responds by rerunning only the stage zero tasks whose output was lost, then retrying stage one. The job carries on. So a failure does not restart the job. But notice the limit. If a task writes to an external system and is retried, that write can happen twice. Spark's guarantees stop at its own boundary. Next, we turn from execution to the abstractions you write it with: RDDs, DataFrames and SQL.

This chapter moves from how Spark runs to what you write, and it starts with the oldest abstraction, the RDD, short for resilient distributed dataset. An RDD is an immutable collection of objects, split into partitions, that remembers how it was built. That memory is its lineage. Every example in this chapter uses the same six order sample, and every result you see was produced by Spark four point zero point one. The code reads the CSV file as lines, takes the first line as the header, drops it, splits each line on commas, and keeps the completed orders. First and count are actions. The filters and the map are transformations, so they only extend the lineage. Count returns four, because orders one, two, four and five are completed, and the file was read as two partitions. Now look at the lineage Spark printed. Read it from the bottom: a Hadoop RDD that reads the file, a mapped RDD of lines, and then a single Python RDD. Three separate Python steps in the code became one entry, because PySpark fuses consecutive Python functions so each record crosses into Python once. That is the misconception to drop. Lineage is not a transcript of your code. It is the dependency chain Spark would replay to rebuild a lost partition, exactly the recovery mechanism from the previous chapter.

When the records of an RDD are two item tuples, Spark treats the first item as a key, and a whole family of by-key operations becomes available. Here, each completed order becomes a pair of store id and amount. Reduce by key with addition then produces one total per store: sixty five for store seven, fifteen for store nine, and eighty for store twelve. Those are the same numbers as the first chapter's partial-sum example, now computed by Spark. Reduce by key is a wide operation, and the lineage shows it. There is a shuffled RDD, and the line marked with a plus and an indent is where one stage ends and the next begins. You can set how many partitions the result has. Passing num partitions equals three gives three output partitions. Now compare group by key. It returns every value for each key, so store seven comes back as a list of forty and twenty five. To get there, every single value has to cross the shuffle. Reduce by key instead adds values inside each partition first, and only sends partial totals. On six rows you cannot see the difference. On two hundred gigabytes you certainly can. That is why grouping and then summing is not equivalent in cost, and why the Spark four point zero point one guide says that for aggregations, reduce by key or aggregate by key will yield much better performance.

Every function you hand to Spark has to travel. Before running a task, Spark serializes the function together with the variables it refers to, its closure, and sends that bundle to the executor. Each task works on its own copy. That explains the first result. The code appends every row to a Python list on the driver, from inside foreach, and afterwards the list is still empty. Each task appended to a copy that disappeared when the task finished. On a cluster that is guaranteed. Even locally, PySpark runs your function in separate Python worker processes, so the driver's list never changes. When tasks need shared, read-only data, such as a lookup from store id to city, use a broadcast variable. Spark ships it once per executor instead of once per task, and the lookup turns the store totals into Hull eighty, Leeds sixty five and York fifteen. For counting things across tasks there are accumulators, which tasks can only add to and only the driver can read. But watch the last example. An accumulator is incremented inside a map. Before any action it reads zero. After one count it reads six, which looks right. After a second count it reads twelve, because the map ran again. The Spark four point zero point one guide is explicit: updates are applied exactly once only inside actions. Inside transformations, recomputation and retries can count the same record more than once.

From here on, the main abstraction is the DataFrame. A DataFrame is a distributed table: rows spread across partitions, with named and typed columns. The crucial difference from an RDD is that Spark knows the schema before it touches the data, and that is what lets the optimizer reason about your query. Watch what the schema changes. Read the orders CSV with only the header option, and Spark returns four columns, every one of them a string, because by default CSV reading does not infer types. Now read it again with an explicit schema, written as a short DDL string. Store id is an integer, amount is a decimal with two places, and the six rows on the right are exactly what Spark returned. Notice one detail in the printed schema. Every column is nullable, even though we never asked for that. When Spark reads files, it treats columns as nullable, so a missing value is possible whatever you declare. Why declare the schema rather than infer it? There is no extra pass over the input. Money stays an exact decimal rather than a floating point approximation. And data of the wrong shape is caught at the boundary, not three joins later. Finally, a misconception people bring from Python. A Spark DataFrame is not a pandas DataFrame. It is not in local memory, nothing is computed until an action, and you never modify it in place.

DataFrame code is built from columns, and a column is not what most people first assume. It is not a container of values. It is an expression, a description of how to compute one value per row. Look at the first line of the code. Multiplying the amount column by a hundred and casting it to an integer produces an object of type Column, and no data has been read. Then three with column calls attach expressions to the orders DataFrame. Amount in pence is the amount times one hundred, cast to an integer, so order one becomes four thousand. Is done compares the status with the string completed, which produces a boolean column. And size uses when and otherwise, Spark's version of an if expression: orders of fifty or more are large, so orders three and five are large and the rest are small. The table shows exactly what Spark returned. These functions come from the pyspark dot sql dot functions module, and there are hundreds of them, from round and upper to coalesce and date arithmetic. They matter because they execute inside the engine, where the optimizer can see them. A plain Python function cannot be seen that way, which is a cost the next chapter measures. Each with column also returns a new DataFrame. The original orders DataFrame is unchanged, which is why chaining reads naturally.

Most batch pipelines are built from three moves. Filtering keeps the rows you want, with where or its alias filter. Projection keeps or computes the columns you want, with select. And grouping with aggregation collapses many rows into one per key. Here they are as the daily summary. The where keeps the completed orders, so six rows become four. Group by store id, then aggregate three ways: a count of orders, the sum of the amounts, and the average rounded to two places. Order by store id makes the output predictable. The result has one row per store. Store seven has two orders, forty plus twenty five, which is sixty five, with an average of thirty two fifty. Stores nine and twelve each have a single order. Now look at the types Spark reported, because they are part of the result. Count is a long, and it is never null. The sum of a decimal with ten digits and two places comes back as a decimal with twenty digits, so a large total cannot overflow the input type. If downstream code expects the original type, that difference matters. One misconception to clear up. Group by on its own does not return a DataFrame. In PySpark it returns a grouped data object, which is only a description of the keys. Nothing is grouped, and nothing can be shown, until you call agg, or one of its shortcuts such as count or sum.

Spark SQL is not a separate engine bolted on the side. Calling spark dot sql with a query string returns an ordinary DataFrame, and the query passes through the same analyser and optimizer as DataFrame code. We checked that directly. The SQL query on the left and the DataFrame version from the previous section produce the identical optimized plan in Spark four point zero point one, once the internal expression numbers are set aside. So choose between them for readability, not speed. To query a DataFrame by name, you register it. Create or replace temp view gives the plan a name in this session, and copies no data at all. When the session ends, the name is gone. A global temporary view lives in a special database called global temp and lasts for the whole application. A table is different again: it is an entry in the catalog that points at data. Save as table writes the data and registers it, and the catalog listing shows daily sales as a managed table and orders as temporary. Managed means Spark owns the files, which live under the warehouse directory. One honest caveat. A plain Spark session uses an in-memory catalog, which our run reported. The files survive a restart, but the table entry does not. Tables outlive the application only when the session is connected to a persistent metastore.

We now have four ways to describe a computation, and they all run on the same engine. So which should you use? For structured data, the default is a DataFrame or SQL, whichever reads better for the task. They give you the optimizer: filters pushed toward the source, unused columns never read, and a join strategy chosen from the data. They are also the only option if your code runs over Spark Connect, because the RDD API is not available there. RDDs still have a place. When records have no useful schema, such as raw text that needs custom parsing, or when you need direct control over how data is partitioned and processed, an RDD is the honest tool. Then there are typed Datasets. They exist in Scala and Java, where each row can be a typed object checked at compile time. The Spark four point zero point one guide states plainly that Python has no Dataset API. In Scala, a DataFrame is simply a Dataset of generic rows. And typed lambdas share a cost with RDDs: the optimizer cannot see inside them. That brings us to the misconception. It is tempting to think RDDs are faster because they are lower level. In PySpark the opposite is usually true. An RDD function moves every record out of the engine and into a Python process and back, while DataFrame built-ins run inside the engine without leaving it.

Every source tells Spark a different amount about types, and the differences show up in your results. Start with CSV, read with no options at all. Both header and infer schema default to false, so Spark returns four string columns named underscore c zero to underscore c three, and the header line becomes a row of data. We wrote the same orders out as JSON and read them back. JSON has no declared types, so Spark infers them from the values. Amount comes back as a double, and store id as a big integer. Read the Parquet copy, and the original types return exactly, decimal with two places and an integer, because Parquet stores the schema inside the files. That leads to a misconception worth testing yourself against. Writing data out and reading it back does not always return the same data. The JSON round trip silently turned an exact decimal into a floating point number. A database read through JDBC is a different kind of source altogether. By default it is a single query over a single connection, so one task does all the work. Add a partition column, bounds and a number of partitions, and Spark issues that many queries in parallel, each hitting the live database. Read the bounds carefully. They only decide how the key range is divided. They do not filter anything, so rows outside the bounds are still read, by the first and last partitions.

Writing looks like a single call, but it produces a structure you need to understand. The code writes the orders as Parquet, partitioned by status, in overwrite mode. On the right is the directory Spark four point zero point one created. It is a folder, not a file. Inside, there is one folder per status value, named status equals cancelled, completed and pending, and inside each a part file written by a task. Notice where the status column went. It is no longer inside the files. It moved into the folder names, and Spark puts it back as a column when the directory is read. The files are compressed with snappy, the default for Parquet, and the underscore success file is a marker that the job finished. Then the code tries to write to the same path again without a mode, and it fails with path already exists. That is the default mode, error if exists, and it is a safety net. The other modes are append, overwrite and ignore, which silently skips the write when data is already there. Now the important caveat, quoted from the documentation: save modes use no locking and are not atomic. Which leads to the misconception. Overwrite does not swap the old data for the new. It deletes the existing data first, then writes. If the job fails half way, you can be left with neither version.

Sooner or later results leave the cluster, and there are two ways that goes wrong. The first is size. Take and limit bring back a bounded number of rows, so take two returns exactly two. Collect brings back every row into the memory of a single process, the driver. To iterate without holding everything at once, to local iterator fetches one partition at a time. Spark also has a guard, spark dot driver dot max result size, one gigabyte by default. If the serialized results of an action exceed it, the job is aborted rather than crashing the driver. The second problem is side effects. Foreach and foreach partition run your function on the executors, inside tasks. If that function calls an external system, for example posting each row to an API, remember the previous chapter. Tasks can be retried, and a retried task repeats every call it already made. So design those calls to be idempotent: use a stable key, prefer upserts over inserts, or let Spark's own writers handle the output. Now the misconception, and it is the most common production bug in this chapter. Collect worked on the sample, so it must be fine. Here the result had three rows. On the full retail workload, the identical line can try to pull hundreds of gigabytes into one process. Aggregate or limit first, then collect what is left.

Let's finish the chapter by reading a complete small pipeline and predicting its result before Spark does. The pipeline filters the orders to completed ones, joins them to the store reference data on store id, groups by city, counts the orders and sums the sales, and sorts by sales from highest to lowest. Trace it by hand. The filter removes order three, which was cancelled, and order six, which is pending, leaving four. The join gives every remaining order its city, and because all three stores appear in the reference data, no order is lost. Grouping by city puts orders one and two together in Leeds, forty plus twenty five, sixty five. York has order four, fifteen. Hull has order five, eighty. Sorted by sales, that is Hull, Leeds, York, and that is exactly what Spark returned. Now the habit worth keeping: check invariants, not just the rows. The sales should total one hundred and sixty, the sum of the completed orders. Four orders went in, so four should be counted. And there should be one row per city. Each of those checks would catch a real bug. Suppose a new store appeared in the orders but not yet in the reference file. The inner join would silently drop its orders, and the total would fall below one hundred and sixty. The next chapter is full of failures like that. One last misconception. Without the order by, the rows might happen to look sorted on a small run, but after a shuffle Spark promises no order at all. Next, we test these pipelines against imperfect data: missing values, bad records, and joins that multiply rows.

Chapter three assumed tidy data. This chapter takes it away, and every result you will see came from running Spark four point zero point one on deliberately messy records. Start with the promise people attach to schemas: declare the types and bad data gets caught. Look at the table. The same JSON values were read twice, once declaring amount as a decimal and once as a double. As a decimal, the quoted string twelve comma fifty became one thousand two hundred and fifty, with no error at all, because the reader treated the comma as a thousands separator. Twelve point five oh five was quietly rounded to twelve point five one. Only the word abc was flagged as corrupt. Declared as a double, every quoted number was rejected instead. So the declared type decides what gets caught, and neither choice caught the real problem: a European decimal comma that made one order a hundred times too large. Schemas also drift. On the second day, the producer added a channel column. A default Parquet read took the schema from one file and simply missed the new column. Merge schema unions the columns, and older rows get null. And when you combine DataFrames yourself, union matches columns by position and fails on a different count, while union by name matches them by name. The lesson: a schema enforces types. It does not check meaning.

Real event files contain records that cannot be parsed. Our file has eleven lines, and the last one is truncated mid-object. What happens depends on the parse mode. Permissive, the default, keeps going: the ten good lines parse, and the broken line is preserved as text in a corrupt record column. Drop malformed also returns ten rows, but the bad line simply disappears, with no trace that it ever existed. Fail fast stops the read with a malformed record error. None of these is right in general. What matters is choosing one deliberately. Then there are nulls, and they cause more wrong answers than broken lines do. Order nine has no status. Filter for status not equal to cancelled, and you get eight rows, not nine, because comparing null with anything gives null, and a filter only keeps rows where the condition is true. The null safe comparison, eq null safe, keeps all nine. The same logic splits the amounts. Six orders are above twenty, three are at or below it, and order eight, with no amount, is in neither group. Aggregates skip nulls too. Count of amount is nine, so the average divides by nine rather than ten. A good pipeline turns this into a policy: route bad rows to a quarantine table with a reason, count them on every run, and alert when the count moves. Because the default mode keeps going, silence does not mean the data was clean.

Spark four changed a default that affects every pipeline: ANSI mode is now on. The migration guide says so directly. To see what it means, look at the table: four expressions, run with ANSI on and then off. Casting the string twelve comma fifty to a decimal now fails with cast invalid input. Adding one to the largest integer fails with arithmetic overflow. Dividing by zero fails with divide by zero. Fitting one two three point four five six into a decimal with four digits fails as out of range. With ANSI off, the same four expressions do not fail. Three return null, and the overflow wraps around to minus two billion, a perfectly valid looking number that is completely wrong. That is why turning ANSI off to make an error go away is the misconception to avoid. The error was telling you about a bad value, and switching it off turns that value into a null or a wrapped number that flows into your totals. If you genuinely want null for bad input, say so per expression. Try cast, try add and try divide return null on purpose, and leave every other expression strict. If a value can exceed the integer range, widen it first: cast to a big integer, then add. And keep money in decimals. Added as doubles, point one plus point two is point three followed by a long tail of digits. As decimals, it is exactly point three.

Joins are where correct-looking pipelines most often produce wrong totals, because a join can change the number of rows. Here are six orders worth one hundred and ninety nine in total, and a store table in which store seven appears twice, once for its original opening and once for its 2025 reopening. Nothing about that table looks broken. Now join. The inner join returns six rows with a sum of two hundred and twenty five. Orders one and two each matched both store seven rows, so their amounts were counted twice. At the same time, order seven, for store fifteen, found no store and disappeared, and so did order twelve, whose store id is null. A left join keeps every order, so it returns eight rows and two hundred and sixty four, still inflated. A left anti join is the quickest way to list the orders that found no match: seven and twelve. The fix is to make the dimension unique before joining. Deduplicate the stores, and the inner join returns four rows and one hundred and sixty. Make three checks habitual. Is the join key unique on the side that should be unique? Do the row count and the sum change across the join in the way you expect? And does the distinct count of the order key stay the same? One more trap. The store table has a row with a null key, but order twelve still did not match it, because null equals null is not true in SQL.

Window functions answer questions that compare a row with its neighbours: the top order per store, a running total, the previous value. Unlike a group by, a window keeps every row. You describe the window with three parts: partition by, which rows belong together; order by, their sequence; and the frame, which rows around the current one to include. Take store seven, where orders two and six are tied at twenty five. Ordered by amount, highest first, row number gives one, two and three. Rank gives one, two, two. Dense rank also gives one, two, two here, and would differ from rank only at the next value. The tied pair is the interesting part. Row number had to put one of them second and the other third, and which one is arbitrary. Run the job again, on different partitions, and the order can change. If a later step keeps only the first row per group, that is a nondeterministic result. The second table shows a subtler effect. Sum the amount over a window ordered by amount, and you might expect a running total of twenty five, then fifty, then ninety. Instead both tied rows show fifty. When a window has an order by and no explicit frame, the default frame is a range up to the current value, and tied rows share it. For a true row by row running total, specify rows between unbounded preceding and the current row. And to make row number deterministic, add a tiebreaker column to the ordering.

Dates look simple until a business day crosses a time zone. Order four happened at eleven thirty at night, universal time, on the first of October. Which day did it happen on? It depends on who is asking. With the session time zone set to UTC, Spark shows eleven thirty and dates it the first. Set the session to London, which is an hour ahead in October, and the same instant shows as half past midnight, dated the second. In New York it is still the evening of the first. So a daily sales report puts this order on a different day depending on one setting, spark dot sql dot session dot time zone. In our run it was never set, so it defaulted to the machine's zone, which happened to be UTC. Set it explicitly, to the zone the business reports in. Spark also has two timestamp types, and they behave differently. A plain timestamp is an instant. It is stored once and displayed in whatever the session zone is. Timestamp N T Z, no time zone, is a wall clock reading that is never shifted. We wrote both from a London session and read them back in UTC. The instant moved to ten thirty. The wall clock stayed at eleven thirty. Finally, not every local time exists. On the twenty ninth of March, London's clocks jump from one to two in the morning. Ask Spark for one thirty that day in London, and it gives you two thirty.

Order events rarely arrive flat. Here each order carries an array of line items, each item a struct with a sku, a quantity and a price, plus a map of attributes such as the sales channel. Reaching inside is straightforward. Items dot sku returns the array of skus, so order one gives tea and mug. The attributes map is read by key, so channel is web for order one. Ask for a key that is not there, such as promo on order two, and you get null rather than an error. Size counts the items: two for order one, one for order two, zero for order four, whose array is empty, and null for order five, whose array is missing altogether. To work with line items, you usually explode the array into one row per item, and this is where row counts change. Explode returned three rows, two from order one and one from order two. Orders four and five vanished completely, because an empty or missing array produces no rows. Explode outer keeps them, with nulls, and returns five. The line totals add up correctly: forty for order one, twenty five for order two. Now the misconception. Suppose you explode first and then join an order level amount back on. Order one has two lines, so its forty dollar amount appears twice. The sum comes out at one hundred and five instead of sixty five. Aggregate at one grain before joining at another.

Sometimes you need logic that you can express in Python in one line, and it is tempting to wrap it in a user defined function. Before you do, look at what the plan says. The same uppercase operation was written three ways. The built-in upper function appears in the plan as a plain projection, inside the engine. The Python UDF adds a node called batch eval python, which means every row is sent out of the engine to a Python worker process and back. The pandas UDF adds arrow eval python instead. It also leaves the engine, but it ships whole columns in Apache Arrow format and hands your function a pandas series, which is far cheaper per row. Now look at what the Python UDF did with our data. Order nine has a null status, which arrives in Python as None, and calling upper on None raised an attribute error that failed the job. The built-in and the pandas version both simply returned null. A second UDF claimed to return a string but actually returned an integer length. There was no error at all. Spark quietly converted it and returned the text nine. So the rule of thumb is: built-in functions first, a pandas UDF when no built-in exists, and a row at a time Python UDF only as a last resort. The underlying reason is the misconception itself. A UDF is not just a function to the engine. It is a black box the optimizer cannot see inside.

Let's put the chapter together on one stream of nine order events, each hiding a problem we have met. One line is truncated. Order four was sent twice, identically. Order two arrived as pending and was later updated to completed. Order eight is completed but has no amount. Order seven belongs to store fifteen, which is missing from the store table. And order four happened at eleven thirty at night, universal time. Start with the naive answer: filter to completed rows and sum them. That gives seven rows and two hundred and five, and it is wrong. Order four is counted twice, and order eight is counted as an order even though there is nothing to add. Now trace the safe pipeline. Parsing with a corrupt record column quarantines one line and parses eight. A row number over each order, newest event first, keeps one event per order, which leaves six orders. The duplicate collapses, and order two keeps its completed version. Keeping completed orders that actually have an amount leaves five, worth one hundred and ninety, and order eight is flagged rather than silently counted. A left join keeps order seven with a null city, so it can be flagged rather than lost. And with the session in London, order four lands on the second of October. Every one of those numbers is an invariant you can check on each run. Next, we look under the hood, at how Spark turns this code into query plans.

This chapter opens the box between your code and its execution. Everything you write, whether DataFrame calls or SQL, becomes a plan before anything runs, and explain shows you that plan. Here is the daily summary query again, now on one million generated orders and fifty stores, and explain extended prints four versions of it. The parsed plan is your code as written. Names such as city carry a leading quote mark, meaning they have not been looked up yet. The analyzed plan has resolved every name against the data's schema and worked out every type, so it can say that sales is a decimal with twenty digits. The optimized plan is the result of rewrite rules. The filter has moved down next to the order data, and columns the query never uses, such as order id, have been pruned away. Finally the physical plan picks concrete operators: a broadcast hash join for the stores, and exchanges where data must move. Read these trees from the bottom up, because the data enters at the leaves. Plain explain prints only the physical plan, and with adaptive execution on, that plan sits inside an adaptive spark plan node, a reminder that it can still change while the job runs. So drop the idea that your code runs as written. Your code is a request. The plan is what actually runs, and the rest of this chapter takes each phase in turn.

The first real work Spark does with your query is analysis. The parsed plan is just structure. Analysis binds each name to something real, a column in the schema, a table in the catalog, a function, and gives every expression a type. Compare the two plans at the top. In the parsed plan, count star and sum of amount are unresolved. After analysis, count star has become count of one, typed as a big integer, and the sum is typed as a decimal with twenty digits, which is where the widened result type from chapter three came from. Now three ways analysis can affect you. Select a misspelled column, amout, and analysis cannot resolve it. The error says so, and helpfully suggests amount. In Classic Spark, this fails the moment you define the DataFrame, before any action. Over Spark Connect, it surfaces later, when the plan reaches the server. Second, compare store id with the string seven, and analysis does not fail. It inserts casts so both sides have the same type, which you can see in the analyzed plan. Third, add one to the status column. That also analyzes, because a string can be cast to a number in principle. It only fails when the data runs and the value completed refuses to become a number. That is the misconception to drop. A query that analyzes is not proven correct. Analysis checks that names and types fit together, not that the values do.

Once the plan is analyzed, the optimizer rewrites it with rules that never change the result, only the cost. Look at the optimized plan. The filter on status now sits beneath the join, right next to the order data, so the join only sees completed orders. The optimizer has also inferred new filters. Because an inner join can never match a null key, it added is not null on store id on both sides. Columns are pruned. The order table has four columns, but the plan reads only three, which shows up as the read schema in the scan. And small arithmetic is folded. In a separate query, amount times two plus three became amount times five before any row was touched. Then comes the physical choice, and for joins it matters most. The store table is tiny, far below the broadcast threshold of ten megabytes, so Spark chose a broadcast hash join. It sends the whole store table to every task and leaves the order data where it is. Disable broadcasting, and the same query becomes a sort merge join. Now both sides are shuffled by store id into two hundred partitions and sorted before they can be merged. That is two extra exchanges for the same answer. One last misconception. Seeing pushed filters in the scan does not mean fewer rows were read. The stage still read all one million rows, because Parquet can only skip whole row groups whose statistics rule them out, and every row group here contained completed orders.

The physical plan is still a description. To run it, Spark generates code. Look at the markers in front of the operators: star and a number in brackets. Every operator marked star two, the scan's row conversion, the filter, the projection, the broadcast join, and the partial aggregate, was fused into a single generated Java function. Instead of passing each row from operator to operator, that function runs one tight loop that reads a row, filters it, joins it and adds it to the running totals. Parquet data arrives in columnar batches, and the column to row step feeds those batches into the loop. Exchanges break the chain. Code cannot be fused across a shuffle or a broadcast, so this query produced three separate code generation subtrees. The second half of execution is memory. The four point zero point one tuning guide describes a unified model. Of each executor's heap, after three hundred mebibytes are reserved, a fraction, point six by default, forms one shared region. Execution memory, used for shuffles, joins, sorts and aggregations, and storage memory, used for cached data, both draw from it. When execution needs space, it can evict cached blocks, but only down to a protected portion, half of the region by default. Storage can never evict execution. So the misconception to drop is that Spark interprets one operator at a time, row by row. Fused operators run as a single loop of generated code.

Exchanges are where you should look first in any plan, because they are where data moves between tasks, and where one stage ends and the next begins. This query has two kinds. The broadcast exchange collects the fifty stores and copies them to every task. It even ran as a job of its own. The hash partitioning exchange routes rows by city so that every city's partial results meet in one place. That is the shuffle. A third kind appeared in the first version of this query, which ended with an order by: a range partitioning exchange, which splits rows into sorted ranges so the output can be globally ordered. Now the mechanics behind a shuffle, as the Spark guide describes them. On the map side, each task writes its output to local disk, organised by the partition each row is headed for. On the reduce side, each task fetches its own partition from every map task's output. Put numbers on it. The map side read one million orders, joined and partially aggregated them, and wrote just two hundred records, fifty cities from each of four tasks, seventeen thousand bytes in total. That is the partial aggregation from chapter two, measured. One misconception to drop. The plan says two hundred partitions, but two hundred tasks did not run. Adaptive execution saw how little data there was and read the whole shuffle as a single coalesced partition, in one task.

Let's finish by putting a plan side by side with what actually happened when it ran. We called collect once, then asked Spark's monitoring API for the jobs and stages it ran. On top is the executed plan, the final version after adaptive execution. Below is the trace. That single collect produced three jobs. Job fourteen built the broadcast: one task that read the fifty store rows. Job fifteen was the map stage: four tasks reading all one million orders and writing two hundred shuffle records. Job sixteen contained two stages. The first was skipped, because its shuffle output already existed from job fifteen, and the second read those two hundred records in a single task. Now match them to the plan. Broadcast query stage zero is job fourteen. Shuffle query stage one is job fifteen. And the coalesced shuffle read explains why the final stage needed only one task. The four read tasks need explaining too. There were eight small Parquet files, and Spark packed them two to a task for four cores. Then check the invariants: fifty rows out, one per store; eight hundred thousand completed orders, eighty percent of the input, as the data was generated; and total sales of thirty six million three hundred and sixty four thousand. The misconception to drop is one action, one job. Under adaptive execution, each query stage can run as a job of its own. Next, we turn this kind of evidence into performance diagnosis.

This chapter is about making a Spark job faster without fooling yourself, and that starts before any tuning. First, correctness. Every change in this chapter is checked against a checksum, here the number of result rows, the order count and the sales total, and a change that alters any of them is not an optimisation. It is a bug. Second, data that looks like production. Every measurement here uses ten million generated orders, enough that the costs we care about actually show up. Third, stated conditions: Spark four point zero point one, in local mode with four cores on a single machine. Now the baseline, the daily summary query from earlier chapters. The very first run took three point eight six seconds. The next three took one point two six, one point zero seven and one point two one, so the median is one point two one. Why was the first run three times slower? The JVM was warming up, the file listing was being built, and query code was being generated and compiled for the first time. None of that repeats on later runs. So the method used throughout this chapter is simple. Run once to warm up and throw the result away. Then run several times and compare medians, never single runs. And notice the spread. The warm runs moved by about eight percent, so any difference smaller than that is noise, not a result.

Once you have a baseline, the next question is where the time goes. Do not guess. The Spark UI's stages tab shows it, and the monitoring REST API returns the same numbers as data, which is how every figure in this chapter was collected. Here is the baseline query, broken into its three stages. Stage eighteen read the fifty stores for the broadcast, and took six milliseconds. Stage twenty one combined the shuffled partial results, and took eight. Stage nineteen took three thousand two hundred and seventy five milliseconds of task time, almost all of the query's three thousand two hundred and eighty nine. That is where to look, and nowhere else is worth tuning. The same row tells you more. It read thirty four point seven megabytes from a dataset of one hundred and thirty eight, because only the needed columns were read. Its four tasks took between six hundred and seventy nine and nine hundred and ninety one milliseconds, an even spread, so there is no skew to chase. Read stage metrics in that order: task time to find the work, the minimum, median and maximum task time to spot skew, and then input, shuffle, spill and garbage collection to learn what kind of cost it is. One trap in reading them. Task time is summed across tasks. Three thousand two hundred and seventy five milliseconds of it ran in about one second of wall clock time, because four cores worked in parallel.

Slow stages are slow for different reasons, and each reason leaves a fingerprint in the metrics. The baseline's big stage spent two thousand five hundred and fifty six of its three thousand two hundred and seventy five milliseconds on the CPU, about seventy eight percent, and only three percent in garbage collection. It is CPU bound, which is healthy for a scan and aggregate. To see a memory problem, we sorted all ten million orders with the driver limited to one gigabyte. The stage spilled six hundred and thirty seven megabytes from memory, a hundred and ninety six of them to disk, meaning sort data did not fit and was written out and read back. Input and output problems look different again. Reading the same orders from two thousand small files needed sixty three read tasks and took almost two seconds, three times as long as thirty two files. And scheduling overhead appears as thousands of tasks that each do almost nothing. Two thousand shuffle partitions produced tasks of about a millisecond each. Now look closer at the spill. Sorting through one partition took twenty two seconds, almost all of it in a single twenty second task. Sorting through eight partitions took eight point one seconds. The total spill was nearly identical. What changed was that eight tasks shared it. So the misconception is that spill always means you need more memory. Here, more partitions cut the time by sixty three percent with exactly the same memory.

Partition count sets how work is divided, and there is no single right number. It depends on how much data each task receives. We ran the same aggregation, ten million orders grouped into fifteen hundred store and day combinations, at four different shuffle partition counts with adaptive execution switched off. Four partitions was fastest, at sixty five hundredths of a second. The default of two hundred took one point three one seconds, and two thousand took almost four. After the shuffle there were only fifteen hundred small groups, so most of those tasks had almost nothing to do and paid only scheduling overhead. Now the opposite case. Sorting all ten million rows moves the whole dataset through the shuffle, and there, one partition took twenty two seconds while eight took eight. Too few partitions forces a few tasks to carry everything. So size partitions by data, not by habit. You want enough tasks to keep every core busy, ideally in a few waves. Spark already splits input files at up to one hundred and twenty eight megabytes. And for shuffle output, adaptive execution coalesces small partitions toward an advisory size of sixty four megabytes. With it switched on, this aggregation used a single task and took seventy seven hundredths of a second, without any manual tuning. The misconception to drop: more partitions does not automatically mean faster. Beyond one task per core, extra partitions add overhead.

Many shuffles are written by hand, with repartition and coalesce, so it pays to know exactly what each one costs. Repartition with a number always shuffles. The plan shows a round robin exchange, and the write produced eight files. Coalesce reduces partitions without any exchange at all, by merging existing ones, so two partitions gave two files. Repartition by a column hashes rows by that column into two hundred partitions. You might expect one file per day, thirty in all, but adaptive execution coalesced the partitions and the write produced only five. If you need one folder per value, partition by on the write is the tool for that, not repartition. Now the trade that surprises people. We needed one output file from eight million completed orders, and did it both ways. Coalesce one produced no shuffle, but it pulled the whole upstream stage into a single task: one task read all ten million rows. Repartition one kept four parallel tasks for the reading and filtering, then shuffled seven hundred and forty nine megabytes into one final task. The two took almost exactly the same time, four point seven three and four point seven six seconds, for entirely different reasons. So the misconception is that coalesce is free. It avoids a shuffle by shrinking the parallelism of the work before it. Repartition only when a later step genuinely needs the new layout.

Joins are often the most expensive operators in a plan, and Spark has several ways to run them. To compare them fairly, we joined ten million orders to a million customers and grouped by customer segment, the same query each time, with the same checksum every time. With adaptive execution off, Spark's default was a sort merge join. It shuffled about a hundred and thirty megabytes, sorted both sides, and took five point four one seconds. A shuffle hash join hint kept the same shuffle but skipped the sort, building a hash table instead, and took three point eight five. A broadcast hint sent the whole customer table to every task, so nothing was shuffled at all, and it was fastest at three point three one. Why did Spark not broadcast on its own? Its estimate for the customer table, with all three columns, was eleven point one eight megabytes, just over the ten megabyte threshold. And here is something that caught us out while measuring. An earlier query that read only the customer id column estimated just three point seven three megabytes, and Spark broadcast it without being asked. So the misconception to drop is that a pair of tables has one join strategy. Spark decides from the estimated size of what the query actually reads, after columns are pruned. Always check the strategy in the executed plan of the exact query you are timing.

Skew is when one key carries far more data than the rest, so the task that owns it runs long while the others sit idle. To measure it, we made a copy of the orders in which store seven holds half of all rows, five point one million of ten million, and joined it to the store table with broadcasting switched off. Detect it in the task times. The join stage's median task took nine hundred milliseconds, but its slowest took almost nineteen hundred. That long maximum is the signature of skew. Then we tried the standard mitigations and measured each one. Adaptive execution has skew join handling, on by default, but it only acts on a partition larger than both five times the median and two hundred and fifty six megabytes. Our skewed partition never reached that, so nothing changed. Lowering the threshold to eight megabytes made adaptive execution split the skewed partition into several tasks. The slowest task fell to six hundred and twenty four milliseconds, and the query to two point two four seconds. Broadcasting the small store table removed the skewed shuffle altogether, and took just over one second. Finally, salting, which adds a random key to spread the hot store across eight partitions. It was the slowest option, three point six seven seconds, and still had a nineteen hundred millisecond task. The misconception is that salting always fixes skew. Here, the real fix was removing the shuffle.

Every action recomputes its plan from the source unless you cache an intermediate result. That makes caching look like an easy win, so let's measure it. We built an enriched dataset, completed orders joined to stores, and ran two aggregations over it, one by city and one by day. Recomputing the enriched data for each aggregation took two point one two seconds in total. Then we cached it. Caching is lazy, so the first count is what actually builds the cache, and it took two point two five seconds on its own. After that, both aggregations together took one point three nine seconds. Add it up. The cached version cost three point six four seconds, against two point one two without it. Caching saved about seven tenths of a second each time the pair of aggregations ran, so it only pays off after roughly three rounds of reuse. The cached data used the default storage level, memory and disk, deserialized, and occupied eighty nine megabytes of memory across four partitions. In the plan, a cached DataFrame appears as an in memory table scan, which is how you confirm that a query actually used it. Remember to unpersist it when you are done, because cached blocks hold storage memory until they are released. So the misconception is that caching always speeds a job up. Used once or twice, this cache made the job slower. Cache what you reuse often, and measure it.

Some of the biggest improvements come not from configuration but from how the data is laid out on disk. We wrote the same ten million orders four ways and queried each with the filter its layout was built for. Partitioned by sale date, a query for one day read three hundred and thirty three thousand rows instead of ten million, under one megabyte instead of twenty eight, and ran in twelve hundredths of a second instead of thirty one. The plan shows why. A partition filter skips every directory except the one for that day. In chapter five, a pushed filter on status read every single row. Here we sorted the data by status within each file before writing it, and the same filter for cancelled orders read only one point two eight million rows. Parquet's row groups record the minimum and maximum of each column, and once the data is clustered, whole row groups can be ruled out. File count matters too. The same data split into two thousand small files needed sixty three read tasks and took nearly two seconds, three times as long as thirty two well-sized files. Every file adds open and listing overhead. So the misconception to drop is that pushdown is automatic and layout does not matter. The pushed filter was identical in both cases. Unsorted, it read ten million rows. Sorted, it read one point two eight million. Layout decides what pushdown can skip.

Adaptive query execution, on by default since Spark three point two, deserves its own look, because it explains several results in this chapter. The optimizer plans from estimates, and estimates can be badly wrong. Here we joined the orders to a filtered customer table, keeping only a few hundred customers. Without cost based statistics, the filter does not shrink the estimate, so Spark still believed the customer side was eleven megabytes and planned a sort merge join. With adaptive execution, Spark ran the customer side first as its own query stage, saw how small it really was, and switched the join to a broadcast hash join. The query went from one point three five seconds to twenty six hundredths. The same mechanism coalesced the aggregation's two hundred shuffle partitions into one task, and, once its threshold was reached, split the skewed partition into nine. All three changes rely on statistics from stages that have already run. That changes how you read plans. Before execution, explain shows adaptive spark plan with is final plan set to false, a starting point. After execution, the final plan shows what actually ran, including the coalesced shuffle reads and the switched join. Compare metrics with the final plan, never the initial one. So the misconception to drop is that explain shows the plan that ran. With adaptive execution on, it shows only the plan Spark started with.

Resources come in executors, each with some cores and some memory. To see how cores translate into speed, we ran the baseline query with one, two and four local cores, five times each. One core took two point eight four seconds. Two cores took one point four seven, almost exactly half. Four cores took one point three three, barely better. The stage metrics explain why. With four cores, the scan ran as four tasks of about a second each, and a stage cannot finish before its slowest task. There was simply not enough independent work to use the extra cores well. On a cluster, the same reasoning applies at scale. Spark executor memory defaults to one gigabyte, and on top of that every executor needs memory overhead outside the JVM heap, ten percent by default with a minimum of three hundred and eighty four mebibytes. Spark executor cores decides how many tasks run concurrently in each executor. Dynamic allocation, off by default, lets Spark add executors when tasks are waiting and remove them when they have been idle, sixty seconds by default. With shuffle tracking, which is on by default, Spark keeps executors that still hold shuffle data that later stages need. So the misconception is that doubling the cores halves the runtime. That only holds while there are enough tasks to keep every core busy, and while no single task dominates its stage.

Let's finish with a full before and after comparison, done the way this chapter recommends: one change at a time, each measured five times, with the checksum checked at every step. The query computes sales by city and day. The starting point combines several mistakes: two thousand small files, adaptive execution off, two thousand shuffle partitions, and broadcasting disabled. Its median was eleven seconds, across more than four thousand tasks. Allowing the store table to be broadcast removed most of the shuffle, sixty five megabytes down to seven and a half, and halved the time to five and a half seconds. Turning adaptive execution on coalesced two thousand tiny shuffle tasks into three, and took us under three seconds. Compacting the input into thirty two files removed sixty read tasks and their overhead, and the query finished in just under one second. At every step the result was identical: fifteen hundred rows, eight million and four hundred and sixty four orders, and the same sales total. Now be honest about the limits. This ran on one machine, with no network, so shuffles were cheaper here than they would be on a cluster. After the first run, the files sat in the operating system's cache. And the starting runs varied from under ten seconds to almost fourteen, which is why we report the median and the spread. So the misconception is that an eleven times speedup here means eleven times in production. The ranking of the fixes transfers. The ratios must be measured again where the job really runs. Next, we leave bounded data behind for data that never stops arriving.

This chapter moves from data that has an end to data that never stops arriving. A bounded input, like yesterday's order files, is fixed: the query reads it, runs once, and finishes. An unbounded input keeps growing, so the useful question changes from what is the answer to how does the answer change as rows arrive. Structured Streaming's model is to treat the stream as a table that keeps getting new rows appended, and to run your query against it incrementally. The code barely changes. You read with read stream instead of read, and write with write stream, giving a checkpoint location. Here the retail order events arrive as four small JSON files, one per micro-batch, and the query sums sales by store. Look at the second column: each batch read only its new rows, three, three, two and two. Yet the result is cumulative. Store seven goes from sixty five, to ninety, to one hundred and thirty, as its orders arrive. After the fourth file, the totals are one hundred and thirty, eighty and one hundred, exactly what a batch query over all ten rows returns. That equality is the contract: a streaming query should give the same answer as the batch query over the data seen so far. The misconception to drop is that each micro-batch recomputes everything from the beginning. It does not. Spark keeps the running totals in state between batches, so the last batch read two rows, not ten. That state is what the rest of this chapter is about.

How does Spark actually run a streaming query? By default it runs a loop of small batch jobs, called micro-batches. Each one goes through the same steps, in the same order. First, the engine asks every source what is new since the last batch, and fixes that range as offsets. Second, before doing any work, it writes those offsets ahead into the checkpoint, so a crash cannot lose track of what this batch was meant to read. Third, it runs the incremental plan on just the new rows. Fourth, it updates the state store, the running totals from the previous section, and writes the result to the sink according to the output mode. Finally, it commits: a record that this batch is finished. Planned, then committed. That pair of records is what makes recovery possible, as we will see in the checkpoint section. You do not have to take this on trust. Every query publishes a progress report, readable as last progress. It shows the batch id, the number of input rows, how long each phase took, the current watermark, the number of rows held in state, and the start and end offsets each source contributed. When a stream falls behind or its state grows, this report is the first place to look. The misconception here is that streaming is a separate engine. It is not. Each micro-batch is an ordinary query, planned by the same optimizer and run by the same executors you met in the earlier chapters.

Every streaming query has two ends, and each end carries a contract. Start with the input. For a query to survive a failure, its source must be able to replay data from a recorded offset. The file source records an index in its own log of which files it has read. Kafka records an offset for each partition. The rate source, used for testing, counts what it generated. The socket source keeps nothing, so if the query fails, the data it already received is gone. It is for experiments only. Now the output. The file sink is exactly-once, because it records which batch wrote which files, and a replayed batch replaces rather than adds. It supports append mode only. Kafka and the foreach sink are at-least-once: if a batch is retried, the same rows can be written again. For each batch hands you a DataFrame and a batch id, and its guarantee is whatever your function provides, which is the subject of section twelve. Console and memory sinks are for debugging and promise nothing. In the retail stream, JSON order files come in and Parquet files go out. Both ends hold up their side, so after a crash Spark can reread the last batch without duplicating anything in the output. The misconception to drop is that exactly-once is something Spark does by itself. It is the combination of a replayable source, a checkpoint that records offsets, and a sink that tolerates replay. Weaken any one of the three and the guarantee is gone.

The trigger decides when micro-batches run. There are four choices. With no trigger set, the default, Spark starts the next micro-batch as soon as the previous one finishes, so latency is roughly one batch duration. A processing time trigger runs batches on a fixed interval, say every two seconds. If a batch takes longer than the interval, the next one starts immediately when it ends; batches never overlap. The available now trigger processes everything that is available when the query starts, possibly in several batches, and then stops. That suits a scheduled job: run it every hour, let it catch up, release the cluster. It still respects source rate limits, and at the end it runs a batch with no data so that the watermark can advance and windows can close. Finally, the continuous trigger is experimental. It keeps long-running tasks open and can reach latencies around a millisecond, but only for map-like queries: selections, projections and filters. Aggregations are not supported, and neither is for each batch. For the retail pipeline, an hourly summary would use available now on a scheduler, while a live dashboard feed would use a two second processing time trigger. The misconception to avoid is that a long trigger interval turns a stream into a batch job. It does not. The query still keeps its state and its checkpoint between runs, and it picks up exactly where it stopped, which a batch job reading the whole input would not.

Every event in a stream carries two different times. Event time is when the thing actually happened, the moment the customer placed the order, and it is a column in the data, written by the producer. Processing time, or arrival time, is when Spark received it. In a perfect pipeline they would be close. In practice they drift apart. Here are the chapter's ten order events. Three of them arrived late: a resent copy of order two arrived fifteen minutes after the order happened, order seven nineteen minutes late, and order nine thirty one minutes late. Now group the ten events into ten minute windows, twice. By when they happened, the counts are six, two, one and one: most of the activity was between nine and ten past nine. By when they arrived, the counts are two, four, two and two, which suggests the busiest period was ten minutes later. Same rows, different answers, and only the first one describes the business. If someone asks for sales between nine and ten past nine, they mean event time. Arrival time is still useful, but it describes the pipeline, its lag and throughput, not the shop. The misconception to drop is that events arrive roughly in order, so arrival time is close enough. Mobile devices go offline, producers retry, and upstream systems resend, as order two shows. Lateness is normal, not exceptional. So a correct streaming query groups by event time, and then needs a rule for how long to wait for late events. That is the next two sections.

Now we follow one event time window through four micro-batches. The query groups the orders into ten minute tumbling windows by event time, sums the amount and counts the orders. It declares a watermark of ten minutes, and it runs in update mode, which sends a window to the sink every time its value changes. Watch the window from nine o'clock to ten past. In batch zero, orders one, two and three arrive, and the window holds eighty, from three orders. In batch one, a resent copy of order two arrives. Nothing removes duplicates yet, so it is counted again: one hundred and five, from four orders. We fix that in section eight. In batch two, order seven arrives. It happened at six minutes past nine, but arrived nineteen minutes late. The watermark in force is seven minutes past nine, which is still before the window's end, so the window is open and order seven is added: one hundred and thirty five. In batch three, order nine arrives, from two minutes past nine. By now the watermark is thirteen minutes past nine, beyond the window's end.
