The window is closed, its state has been removed, and order nine is dropped. The progress report counts it: rows dropped by watermark, one. Notice the misconception this exposes. Order nine was thirty one minutes late, order seven nineteen. Whether a late event is kept depends on the watermark when it arrives, not on how late it is in isolation. The next section explains how that watermark moves.

A watermark is how Spark decides that a window is final. Its value is the latest event time seen so far, minus the delay you declare, here ten minutes. It is updated between batches and it never moves backwards. In our events, after order three at eight minutes past nine, the watermark becomes two minutes to nine. After order five, seven past nine. After order six, thirteen past. After order eight, twenty one past. Now run the same windowed query in append mode, which writes each window exactly once, only when it can no longer change. Nothing reaches the sink at first. At batch five the watermark reaches thirteen past nine, past the end of the nine o'clock window, so that window is written: one hundred and thirty five, from five orders. At batch seven, the ten past window is written: one hundred and forty, from two orders. Batches one, three, five and seven had no new data at all. Available now ran them only to move the watermark forward so windows could close. And because closed windows leave state, the state never held more than three rows. Read the guarantee carefully, because it holds in one direction only. Data that arrives within the declared delay is never dropped. Data later than that may be dropped, but is not guaranteed to be; it depends on batch timing. So the delay is a trade. A longer delay keeps more late events, but every window is written later and more state is kept in memory. A shorter delay gives fresher results and less state, and loses more late data.

Some streaming operations need to remember the past. Aggregations keep running totals, deduplication keeps the ids it has already seen, and stream to stream joins keep rows waiting for a match. That memory is called state. It lives per partition in a state store on the executors, and it is saved with every checkpoint. The question to ask of any stateful query is: what lets Spark forget? Here we remove the resent copy of order two, in two ways. Drop duplicates on order id, with no watermark, has to remember every id it has ever seen, because a duplicate could arrive at any time. The state goes three, five, seven, nine, growing with every order. Drop duplicates within watermark keeps an id only while its event time is within the watermark, so old ids are removed. Its state goes three, five, five, four. Both versions removed the second order two. But notice what else changed. With the watermark, orders seven and nine were dropped as well, because their event times were already behind the watermark when they arrived. The window aggregation in the last section, with its own state, still accepted order seven. So the watermark bounds state, and it also decides which late events count. The misconception to drop is that a small stream has small state. State grows with the number of distinct keys over the whole life of the query, not with the size of each batch. At two hundred gigabytes of order events a day, deduplication without a watermark grows without limit, until the executors run out of memory.

The output mode decides what a micro-batch sends to the sink. Run the same windowed query three ways and compare, file by file. In append mode, nothing appears for the first two files, because no window is final yet. After the third file, the nine o'clock window is written once, at one hundred and thirty five. After the fourth, the ten past window, at one hundred and forty. Each row is written once and never changes, which is what a file sink needs. In update mode, each batch sends only the windows that changed. The nine o'clock window appears three times, at eighty, one hundred and five and one hundred and thirty five, so the sink must be able to overwrite a row by its key, like a database table. In complete mode, every batch rewrites the whole result: one window, then two, three and four. Look at the last row. Complete mode counted order nine, which the other modes dropped, and the nine o'clock window ended at one hundred and forty from six orders. Complete mode must be able to reproduce the entire result, so it keeps all state, and the watermark cannot drop any of it. The compatibility rules follow from this. Append with an aggregation needs a watermark, so Spark knows when a row is final. Complete works only for aggregations. The file sink accepts append only. The misconception to drop is that output mode is a formatting choice. It changes when rows appear, which late events count, and how much state the query must keep forever.

Joins in a stream come in two kinds. A stream static join joins each micro-batch to a table that does not stream, here the order events to the stores table. Every batch's new rows are joined to the stores, and no join state is needed. But it joins what arrives, duplicates included: the resent copy of order two was joined to Leeds twice. Deduplicate first if that matters. A stream to stream join is harder, because either side can arrive first. Here orders join to payments. Spark must keep orders in state until their payment arrives, and payments until their order arrives. Without a limit, that state grows forever. So we declare a watermark on each side and a time bound in the join condition: the payment must come within fifteen minutes of the order. Together they tell Spark when a row can no longer match and can be removed. For inner joins these are optional but strongly advised. For outer joins they are required, because Spark can only emit the unmatched row once it knows no match is coming. Now the result. Order one was paid two minutes later and joined in batch zero. Order four, also two minutes, joined in batch two. Order two was paid sixteen minutes later and order three thirty two minutes later. Both fall outside the bound, so they never joined. Along the way the join held up to eleven rows of state. The misconception to drop is that a streaming join waits until both sides arrive. It waits only as long as the bound allows.

The checkpoint directory is the query's memory, and it is what makes a restart continue instead of starting over. Look inside one after two batches. Offsets zero and one record what each batch was meant to read; they are written first, before the batch runs. Commits zero and one record that both batches finished. The sources folder holds the file source's log of files read, the state folder holds the store totals, and metadata holds the query id. Offsets one contains log offset one: the files up to index one have been taken. Now restart the query with the same checkpoint location. Spark reads the last offset and the last commit, sees that batch one finished, and starts batch two, reading only the two new rows of the third file. If the crash had come between writing offsets one and writing commits one, Spark would re-run batch one with exactly the same range. That replay is safe only if the sink tolerates it, which is the next section. A checkpoint also fixes the query's shape. The guide lists which changes are allowed between restarts. Adding or removing a filter is fine. Adding a source, or changing its type, is not. Pointing a file sink at a new path is not. Changing the grouping keys or aggregates is not, because the saved state no longer matches the new schema. The misconception to drop is that a checkpoint is a backup you can reuse for a new query. It belongs to one query shape. For an incompatible change, start a new checkpoint and plan how to backfill.

Here is the case that decides whether a pipeline double counts. After a failure, Spark replays the batch that was planned but not committed. It uses the same batch id and, because the source is replayable, the same input rows. What the replay does to the output depends entirely on the sink. We use for each batch, which hands your function each batch's DataFrame and its batch id. The stream has three batches with eight distinct orders. The query crashes after writing batch one, but before committing it, and is then restarted. The first writer appends every attempt to a Parquet log. Batch one is written twice, and the sink ends with eleven rows, only eight of them distinct. Every downstream total is now wrong. The second writer overwrites the batch's own location, a folder named by the batch id. The replay replaces what the first attempt wrote, and the sink ends with exactly eight rows. That is idempotency: doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. There are two common ways to get it. Write each batch to a place derived from its batch id, as here, or merge by key. Or record the last batch id you wrote in the target system, and skip a batch already done. If your function writes to several places, each write needs the same care. The misconception to drop is that because Spark is exactly-once, your sink is too. Spark gives at-least-once execution of each batch. Exactly-once effect comes from pairing that with a replayable source and an idempotent sink.

Let's put the whole chapter into one timeline, and state the assumptions first. The source is files, so it can replay. The query declares a ten minute watermark, removes duplicates within the watermark, groups into ten minute windows, and appends to a file sink, running with the available now trigger. Now trace every event. Orders one, two and three fall in the nine o'clock window. Orders four and five fall in the ten past window. The resent copy of order two arrives in file two and is removed as a duplicate, because its id is still in state. Order seven happened at six past nine but arrived at twenty five past, when the watermark was already seven past, so it is dropped. Order nine, from two past nine, arrives even later and is dropped too. Orders six and eight start the twenty past and half past windows, which stay open. After file four, the watermark is twenty one minutes past nine. The sink holds two final rows: the nine o'clock window, eighty from three orders, and the ten past window, one hundred and forty from two orders. Now add a crash anywhere in this timeline. Spark replays the uncommitted batch from the checkpoint, the file sink keeps each window once, and the final output is the same. Finally, the limitation. Order seven was a real sale, and it is missing from these totals. A longer watermark would keep it, at the cost of later output and more state. Streaming adds state that must be bounded, recovery that must be designed, and outputs that run for months. Next, we connect those obligations to running Spark in production.
